content:
UPDATE: I checked my Message Filter settings and found some possible causes. I had checked "Manually Run", "Periodically", and "Getting New Mail" all at the same time. This seemed to trigger a data-handling conflict under a heavy load.

Looking at my macOS diagnostic logs, the failure unfolded in just 2.25 seconds: - 10:22:33.14: The network hub is acutely overloaded by a sudden flood of IMAP data. - 10:22:33.65: iCloud security hits a timeout because it cannot process the authentication tokens rapidly enough. - 10:22:35.39: Local KeySync triggers a hard lock, permanently freezing the application process.

Making these filter checkbox options mutually exclusive could maybe prevent users from accidentally creating conflicting background loops.

The real, structural solution though is, Mozilla could implement something like decoupling the startup of the visual interface, downloading e-mail, and the background filtering tasks at the same instant.

More testing would need to be done to find the root cause.

[Note: Troubleshooting and formatting done with the assistance of a free AI tool based on my local macOS Console logs and reconstruction of the events.]

In Thunderbird

  • Settings > Privacy & Security
  • Web Content
  • Select 'Accept cookies from sites'
  • Accept third party cookies
  • click on exceptions button and add this: https://accounts.google.com
  • click on 'Save Changes'

It would be useful to know if you set up Imap or POP Gmail IMAP incoming server

Release is the bleeding edge where you get all the new features fortnightly, along with their inherent bugs that come with all new software features. content:
Lts look at this error message you posted 

"Sending of the message failed. An error occurred while sending mail: Outgoing server (SMTP) error.  The server responded:

resomta-c2p-555442.sys.comcast.net resomta-c2p-555442.sys.comcast.net ESMTP server not available (9009/146.70.230.100)."

SO resomta-c2p-555442.sys.comcast.net resomta-c2p-555442.sys.comcast.ne is comcasts mail server which has generated the response. 

ESMTP server not available (9009/146.70.230.100)."

This part tells us you are sending (ESMTP) and that the server is not available for some reasons that the server identified as 9009 and gives your IP address as 146.70.230.100

I have no idea what the 9009 means to Comcast of the server in question. but a quick google of the address shows https://www.netify.ai/resources/ips/146.70.230.100

It is fairly common in the USA for providers to only allow you to send mail if you connect to their servers from their network. Your VPN is not part of their network so I would guess you can not send mail unless you disable the VPN. The use of a VPN is a growing thing, but generally they do very little for the average user to improve their security but they do an excellent job of masking your geo location which means any service that relies on knowing it will have issues. Like your ISP mail and even google mail or Facebook et. al. but often you have a VPN to mask you geo location and a GPS location on the same device handing out your location to meters. Portable devices routinely use GPS to locate themselves and the user and will report that if asked the right way so you have to ask what the benefit of the VPN is to you when you elect to use one.

Windows offers enough bread crumbs that you and the device can still be identified even with a VPN. A VPN is not the panacea for anonymity most folk think they are. See this recent news article on identifying an offender despite VPN use, https://cyberinsider.com/microsoft-windows-telemetry-identified-hacker-despite-vpn-use/

If the FBI can do it, so can just about everyone else.
